sets.title: Anthem for Doomed Youth
sets.author: Wilfred Owen
sets.source: Anthem for Doomed Youth, in Poems (ed. Siegfried Sassoon), Chatto & Windus, 1920 (written 1917)
sets.headnote: Wilfred Owen, a British officer on the Western Front, drafted this sonnet in 1917 at Craiglockhart War Hospital, where he was being treated for shell shock. He was killed in November 1918 and the poem was published after his death.
sets.body:
What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?
— Only the monstrous anger of the guns.
Only the stuttering rifles' rapid rattle
Can patter out their hasty orisons.
No mockeries now for them; no prayers nor bells;
Nor any voice of mourning save the choirs,—
The shrill, demented choirs of wailing shells;
And bugles calling for them from sad shires.

What candles may be held to speed them all?
Not in the hands of boys, but in their eyes
Shall shine the holy glimmers of goodbyes.
The pallor of girls' brows shall be their pall;
Their flowers the tenderness of patient minds,
And each slow dusk a drawing-down of blinds.

pair.title: The Man He Killed
pair.author: Thomas Hardy
pair.source: The Man He Killed, in Time's Laughingstocks and Other Verses, Macmillan, 1909 (first published 1902)
pair.headnote: Thomas Hardy wrote this dramatic monologue during the Boer War (1899–1902). The speaker is an ordinary working man; a nipperkin is a small measure of drink, and to 'list is to enlist.
pair.body:
“Had he and I but met
By some old ancient inn,
We should have sat us down to wet
Right many a nipperkin!

“But ranged as infantry,
And staring face to face,
I shot at him as he at me,
And killed him in his place.

“I shot him dead because —
Because he was my foe,
Just so: my foe of course he was;
That's clear enough; although

“He thought he'd 'list, perhaps,
Off-hand like — just as I —
Was out of work — had sold his traps —
No other reason why.

“Yes; quaint and curious war is!
You shoot a fellow down
You'd treat if met where any bar is,
Or help to half-a-crown.”

He starts confidently, "I shot him dead because —", but the dash breaks the line and all he can do is repeat himself: "Because he was my foe." The halting syntax shows that the official reason for killing doesn't satisfy him.

questions.model:
Line by line, Owen's sonnet holds the rituals of a Christian funeral up against the battlefield and finds that the soldiers get none of them. The opening question, "What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?", sets up the contrast. Bells honour the individual dead, but the simile reduces the soldiers to animals slaughtered en masse. The answer swaps ritual for noise: "Only the monstrous anger of the guns." The alliteration and onomatopoeia of "the stuttering rifles' rapid rattle" imitate gunfire, and "patter out their hasty orisons" makes prayer mechanical and rushed. Even the choir becomes "The shrill, demented choirs of wailing shells", personification that turns the artillery into a mad parody of mourning, and conventional religion is dismissed as "mockeries".

The sestet answers the second question by moving the rituals home, to the people left behind. Candles become "the holy glimmers of goodbyes" in boys' eyes, the funeral cloth becomes "The pallor of girls' brows", and "each slow dusk a drawing-down of blinds" turns a household mourning custom into grief that repeats every day. The sonnet moves from the clamour of the octave to this hushed, slow ending, and that movement is Owen's point: the only real funeral rites are the private sorrow of the people who loved the dead.

questions.model:
Both poems challenge comfortable public attitudes to war, but they come at them from opposite directions. Owen, an officer grieving for his men, attacks the belief that soldiers die nobly and are honoured. Hardy, speaking as an ordinary infantryman, attacks the belief that the man you kill is truly your enemy. Owen's challenge is elegiac and angry; Hardy's is quiet and ironic, and all the more unsettling for being so plain.

The first difference is how each sees the soldier. Owen's soldiers are an anonymous mass, "these who die as cattle", denied even individual burial rites, and that dehumanisation is what enrages him. Hardy does the reverse. He gives the enemy back his individuality. The man he killed turns out to mirror the speaker, someone who "thought he'd 'list, perhaps, / Off-hand like — just as I — / Was out of work". The dashes imitate a mind slowly realising that the "foe" was just another poor man, and the accepted category of enemy falls apart.

Voice and form sharpen each challenge. Owen uses the elevated sonnet, the form of love and praise, and fills it with "monstrous anger" and "wailing shells", so the form itself turns ironic: this is an anthem that refuses to celebrate. Hardy's short, ballad-like quatrains and everyday diction, "Right many a nipperkin!", sound like a conversation in a pub, not a lament. The jaunty rhythm clashes with the subject, and the hesitation in "because — / Because he was my foe" exposes the official justification as hollow.

The endings show the difference most clearly. Owen finishes in mourning, "each slow dusk a drawing-down of blinds", and moves us to grieve for those at home. Hardy finishes with understatement: "Yes; quaint and curious war is!" The adjectives are deliberately, absurdly inadequate, so we have to supply the moral judgement the speaker can't. Owen makes us feel what war costs; Hardy makes us question its logic. Between them they take apart both the glory of dying and the justice of killing.

sets.title: Crossing the Bar
sets.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
sets.source: Crossing the Bar, in Demeter and Other Poems, Macmillan, 1889
sets.headnote: Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Poet Laureate of Britain, wrote this short lyric in 1889, aged eighty, and asked that it be placed at the end of all collections of his poems. The 'bar' is a sandbank across a harbour mouth.
sets.body:
Sunset and evening star,
And one clear call for me!
And may there be no moaning of the bar,
When I put out to sea,

But such a tide as moving seems asleep,
Too full for sound and foam,
When that which drew from out the boundless deep
Turns again home.

Twilight and evening bell,
And after that the dark!
And may there be no sadness of farewell,
When I embark;

For tho' from out our bourne of Time and Place
The flood may bear me far,
I hope to see my Pilot face to face
When I have crost the bar.

pair.title: Up-Hill
pair.author: Christina Rossetti
pair.source: Up-Hill, in Goblin Market and Other Poems, Macmillan, 1862
pair.headnote: Christina Rossetti was an English poet of strong religious faith. This poem, first published in 1861, is a dialogue between a traveller and an unnamed guide.
pair.body:
Does the road wind up-hill all the way?
Yes, to the very end.
Will the day's journey take the whole long day?
From morn to night, my friend.

But is there for the night a resting-place?
A roof for when the slow dark hours begin.
May not the darkness hide it from my face?
You cannot miss that inn.

Shall I meet other wayfarers at night?
Those who have gone before.
Then must I knock, or call when just in sight?
They will not keep you standing at that door.

Shall I find comfort, travel-sore and weak?
Of labour you shall find the sum.
Will there be beds for me and all who seek?
Yea, beds for all who come.

questions.model: Tennyson imagines death as a calm sea voyage, so dying becomes a departure rather than an ending. A "clear call" at sunset summons the speaker, and death is simply the moment "When I put out to sea." He prays for "no moaning of the bar", the sound of waves breaking over the sandbank, which doubles as the moaning of mourners; he wants a crossing without turbulence or grief. Instead he asks for a tide "Too full for sound and foam", an image of quiet completeness, and the soul that "drew from out the boundless deep / Turns again home", as if death were a return to where life began. The voyage ends with the "Pilot", a metaphor for God, whom he hopes to see "face to face", and the metaphor becomes a statement of faith.

questions.model:
Both poets picture death as the end of a journey that leads to rest with God, but they put the weight in different places. Tennyson's speaker looks forward with calm, almost eager acceptance to the voyage itself. Rossetti's traveller looks back on how hard life has been and needs to be reassured that rest will come.

The journeys show the difference. In Text 1 it is a sea crossing begun at sunset, and all the speaker asks is that it be gentle: "may there be no moaning of the bar, / When I put out to sea". Death is a short passage over a sandbank. In Text 2 the journey is life itself, a road that winds "up-hill all the way", lasting "From morn to night". Rossetti stresses how long and laborious living is, and death is the "resting-place" reached at nightfall.

Voice reinforces these attitudes. Tennyson's single speaker uses exclamations and prayerful wishes, "And may there be no sadness of farewell", and sounds composed and hopeful. Rossetti splits the voice into an anxious questioner, "Shall I find comfort, travel-sore and weak?", and a calm guide, so doubt is dramatised and then answered.

Both end in faith. Tennyson hopes "to see my Pilot face to face", a personal meeting with God. Rossetti's guide promises company and shelter: "Those who have gone before" and "beds for all who come". Tennyson's comfort is individual and visionary, Rossetti's shared and domestic, but both turn death from something to fear into a homecoming.

sets.title: The Tyger
sets.author: William Blake
sets.source: The Tyger, in Songs of Innocence and of Experience, 1794
sets.headnote: William Blake was an English poet, painter and engraver who printed and hand-coloured his own books. This poem appears in Songs of Experience, a companion to his earlier Songs of Innocence, which contains a poem called 'The Lamb'.
sets.body:
Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
What immortal hand or eye,
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

In what distant deeps or skies,
Burnt the fire of thine eyes?
On what wings dare he aspire?
What the hand, dare seize the fire?

And what shoulder, & what art,
Could twist the sinews of thy heart?
And when thy heart began to beat,
What dread hand? & what dread feet?

What the hammer? what the chain,
In what furnace was thy brain?
What the anvil? what dread grasp,
Dare its deadly terrors clasp!

When the stars threw down their spears
And water'd heaven with their tears:
Did he smile his work to see?
Did he who made the Lamb make thee?

Tyger Tyger burning bright,
In the forests of the night:
What immortal hand or eye,
Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?

questions.model: Blake makes the tiger a living flame, terrifying and beautiful at once. The opening address, "Tyger Tyger, burning bright", makes its striped coat glow like fire, and against "the forests of the night" that brightness looks even more vivid and more threatening, as if the tiger were the only light in a dark, dangerous world. Fire also suggests energy and destruction. In the second stanza the speaker wonders where "Burnt the fire of thine eyes", so even the tiger's gaze is fierce. And "What the hand, dare seize the fire?" suggests that making the tiger took a daring, even dangerous creator. The fire imagery shapes both the beast and the mysterious power behind it.

questions.model:
Blake explores the tiger's creation through a relentless run of questions that never get answered, and through the extended metaphor of a blacksmith's forge. Creation becomes violent physical labour by a power the speaker can neither see nor understand.

The forge dominates the fourth stanza: "What the hammer? what the chain, / In what furnace was thy brain? / What the anvil? what dread grasp". The creator is a smith beating the tiger into shape, and the tiger's brain is heated and hammered like metal. The short, heavily stressed lines and the repeated "what" fall like hammer blows, and the hard sounds of "dread" and "deadly" make the work menacing. Even the body is forged: the creator must "twist the sinews of thy heart", a verb full of strain and force.

The questions build to the most disturbing one: "Did he who made the Lamb make thee?" If the gentle lamb and the fierce tiger share a maker, we have to ask how a good creator could make something so terrible. The final stanza repeats the first but changes "Could" to "Dare", so the last question shifts from whether the creator was able to whether he had the nerve. The poem ends with no answers, and the creator stays a mystery.

questions.model:
I find the claim largely persuasive. Blake gives the tiger an intense physical presence, but every image of the animal turns into a question about its maker, and the real subject is the unsettling possibility that one creator is responsible for both innocence and ferocity.

The tiger is certainly vivid. It is "burning bright", with fiery eyes, a heart of twisted "sinews" and a brain formed in a "furnace". Yet Blake never shows it hunting or moving; he shows it being made. The repeated question, "What immortal hand or eye, / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?", moves our attention from the creature to the "immortal hand" behind it. "Fearful symmetry" is the poem's central paradox: the tiger's perfect design inspires awe and terror together, so its beauty and its danger can't be separated.

The climax confirms that the poem is about good and evil. "Did he who made the Lamb make thee?" recalls the lamb of Songs of Innocence, a traditional symbol of Christ and gentleness. If one God made both, then the violence of experience is part of the divine plan, and the speaker can't tell whether that God "smile[d] his work to see". The image just before it, "When the stars threw down their spears / And water'd heaven with their tears", echoes a fall or rebellion on a cosmic scale, widening the poem from zoology to theology.

The structure deepens the mystery. The final stanza repeats the first almost word for word, making a circle with no answer, but one word changes: "Could frame" becomes "Dare frame". The question is no longer whether such a creation was possible, but how anyone dared attempt it, which puts the stress on moral power rather than physical power.

It would go too far to say the animal doesn't matter. Without its concrete, dazzling energy the questions would be abstract. But Blake uses the tiger as a symbol to confront how beauty, terror and goodness can exist in the same creation, so the claim holds.

sets.title: I wandered lonely as a cloud
sets.author: William Wordsworth
sets.source: I wandered lonely as a cloud, in Poems, Longman, 1815 (first version published 1807)
sets.headnote: William Wordsworth was an English Romantic poet who lived in the Lake District. The poem draws on a walk he took with his sister Dorothy beside Ullswater in April 1802; this is his revised version of 1815.
sets.body:
I wandered lonely as a cloud
That floats on high o'er vales and hills,
When all at once I saw a crowd,
A host, of golden daffodils;
Beside the lake, beneath the trees,
Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.

Continuous as the stars that shine
And twinkle on the milky way,
They stretched in never-ending line
Along the margin of a bay:
Ten thousand saw I at a glance,
Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.

The waves beside them danced; but they
Out-did the sparkling waves in glee:
A poet could not but be gay,
In such a jocund company:
I gazed—and gazed—but little thought
What wealth the show to me had brought:

For oft, when on my couch I lie
In vacant or in pensive mood,
They flash upon that inward eye
Which is the bliss of solitude;
And then my heart with pleasure fills,
And dances with the daffodils.

questions.model:
The final stanza turns a description of a beautiful scene into a reflection on how memory and imagination make it last. The first three stanzas are in the past tense and record what the speaker saw. The last moves into a habitual present: "For oft, when on my couch I lie". The real value of the daffodils, it turns out, lies not in the moment but in remembering it.

The third stanza sets this up. The speaker admits that he "gazed—and gazed—but little thought / What wealth the show to me had brought". The dashes slow the line to suggest absorbed looking, and the financial metaphor "wealth" implies the experience was being stored up to draw on later.

In the final stanza he spends it. The daffodils "flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude". Imagination becomes a kind of sight, and solitude, the source of loneliness in the first line, is now "bliss". The last line, where his heart "dances with the daffodils", completes the change: he now joins the dance he once only watched. The poem ends with a changed self, not a picture.

questions.model:
The poem suggests that nature does more than please the individual. It gets into the mind, heals loneliness and becomes a permanent part of who you are.

The relationship starts with separation. The speaker "wandered lonely as a cloud", a simile that puts him in the landscape but drifting above it, cut off from people. The daffodils offer company straight away: they are "a crowd, / A host", so nature answers human loneliness with community. The second stanza makes this vast. The flowers are "Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way", and the exaggeration "Ten thousand saw I at a glance" suggests an abundance that links one lakeside to the whole cosmos. The individual is small, but he is part of an ordered, joyful universe.

In the third stanza looking becomes feeling: "A poet could not but be gay, / In such a jocund company". The joy is almost involuntary, as if nature's mood simply passes into the human heart. Yet the poem insists the deepest relationship forms later, in memory. Through "that inward eye", the daffodils become part of his inner life and come back whenever he is "In vacant or in pensive mood".

Put together, this is the Romantic belief that nature and imagination work as partners. The individual doesn't just look at nature; he absorbs it. By the last line, where his heart "dances with the daffodils", the line between self and landscape has dissolved, and nature has become a lasting source of joy that transforms solitude itself.

sets.title: Futility
sets.author: Wilfred Owen
sets.source: Futility, in Poems (ed. Siegfried Sassoon), Chatto & Windus, 1920 (first published in The Nation, 1918)
sets.headnote: Wilfred Owen wrote this short lyric in 1918 while serving in the First World War; it was one of only five poems published in his lifetime. A soldier has died in the snow, and his comrades carry him into the sunlight.
sets.body:
Move him into the sun—
Gently its touch awoke him once,
At home, whispering of fields half-sown.
Always it woke him, even in France,
Until this morning and this snow.
If anything might rouse him now
The kind old sun will know.

Think how it wakes the seeds—
Woke once the clays of a cold star.
Are limbs, so dear-achieved, are sides
Full-nerved, still warm, too hard to stir?
Was it for this the clay grew tall?
—O what made fatuous sunbeams toil
To break earth's sleep at all?

The speaker remembers that the sun "wakes the seeds" and "Woke once the clays of a cold star", picturing it bringing life to a barren planet. The soldier's body is the result of that enormous process: his limbs are "so dear-achieved", the product of ages of growth. That leads to an unbearable question: "Was it for this the clay grew tall?" If life evolved only to be destroyed in war, creation looks pointless. The final question calls the sunbeams "fatuous", meaning foolish, so the "kind old sun" of the first stanza is now being mocked. One death has made the speaker doubt the purpose of everything.

questions.model:
Owen shapes this two-stanza lyric so that its form traces the speaker's collapse from tender hope into anguished questioning.

The first stanza is built on gentle statements and a soft command. "Move him into the sun—" is quiet, and "Gently" at the start of the next line slows us down. The syntax is calm and narrative, recalling home and routine, and "Always it woke him, even in France," stresses habit and continuity. Then "Until this morning and this snow" breaks it. The monosyllables and the repeated "this" pin down the moment of death, and the cold "snow" works against the warmth of the sun. The stanza ends in tentative faith, "The kind old sun will know", but "If anything" has already admitted doubt.

Sound adds to the unease. Owen uses half-rhyme throughout: "once" with "France", "seeds" with "sides", "star" with "stir". The near-misses give the poem a muted, slightly off music, as if harmony itself has failed, which fits a world where the sun can't do its job.

In the second stanza statements give way to questions. The speaker asks whether limbs "Full-nerved, still warm" are "too hard to stir", and the pauses and piled-up adjectives carry desperate disbelief. The questions grow larger and more bitter: "Was it for this the clay grew tall?" The last one breaks off with a dash and a cry, "—O what made fatuous sunbeams toil / To break earth's sleep at all?", and the half-rhyme of "tall", "toil" and "all" sounds like a dying fall. The poem ends with despair, not an answer, and its form mirrors a faith shaken beyond repair.

sets.title: When I have fears that I may cease to be
sets.author: John Keats
sets.source: When I have fears that I may cease to be (written 1818), in Life, Letters, and Literary Remains of John Keats (ed. R. M. Milnes), 1848
sets.headnote: John Keats, an English Romantic poet, wrote this sonnet in January 1818, aged twenty-two. He had trained as a surgeon and had nursed his mother and brother through tuberculosis; he died of the disease himself in 1821.
sets.body:
When I have fears that I may cease to be
Before my pen has glean'd my teeming brain,
Before high-piled books, in charactery,
Hold like rich garners the full ripen'd grain;
When I behold, upon the night's starr'd face,
Huge cloudy symbols of a high romance,
And think that I may never live to trace
Their shadows, with the magic hand of chance;
And when I feel, fair creature of an hour,
That I shall never look upon thee more,
Never have relish in the faery power
Of unreflecting love;—then on the shore
Of the wide world I stand alone, and think
Till love and fame to nothingness do sink.

questions.model:
Keats writes this Shakespearean sonnet as one long sentence, and fear piles up clause by clause until the couplet releases it. The repeated time clauses, "When I have fears", "When I behold" and "And when I feel", keep delaying the main verb, so we are held in suspense just as the speaker is held in anxiety.

Each quatrain adds a new loss. The first fears losing poetic achievement, the "high-piled books" he'll never write; the second, losing imaginative vision, the "Huge cloudy symbols of a high romance" he may never "trace"; the third, losing love, the "fair creature of an hour". The fears move from public ambition to private feeling and get more personal as they go.

The turn comes late, halfway through line 12: "—then on the shore / Of the wide world I stand alone". The dash marks the main clause we have been waiting for, and the enjambment pushes us over the line break to the edge of the "wide world", where he stands alone facing the sea. The couplet finishes the sentence: he thinks "Till love and fame to nothingness do sink." Inverting the syntax puts "sink" at the very end, so the rhythm itself drops. The structure turns fear into a contemplative calm. Facing death, he sees that love and fame matter less than he thought.

questions.model:
The poem presents the clash between desire and mortality very effectively. Keats makes desire so rich and sensuous that the threat of losing it really stings, and then he ends with a resolution that is ambiguous rather than comforting.

Desire comes through images of fullness. His mind is a "teeming brain", his future books are "rich garners" full of "ripen'd grain", and the night sky offers "Huge cloudy symbols of a high romance". Even love has "faery power", a magical, carefree force he calls "unreflecting". Everything he wants is abundant and intense. Against this, mortality arrives in the stark opening phrase "cease to be", and transience in the beloved, a "fair creature of an hour". The gap between endless aspiration and limited time is the poem's central tension, and the repeated "Never" in lines 10 and 11 hammers home what death will take.

The ending is the poem's strongest feature because it refuses easy comfort. Standing "on the shore / Of the wide world", he faces that vastness alone, and love and fame "to nothingness do sink". You can read this as a hard-won calm, where facing death frees him from ambition, or as despair, where everything he values dissolves. The ambiguity is honest, and it leaves the conflict feeling open rather than neatly solved.

Knowing that Keats had watched his mother and brother die of tuberculosis, and would die himself at twenty-five, makes the poem deeply poignant. But it doesn't need the biography to work. The precise imagery and controlled structure make the struggle between longing and limits universal, and that is why it succeeds.

sets.title: The Lake Isle of Innisfree
sets.author: W. B. Yeats
sets.source: The Lake Isle of Innisfree, in The Countess Kathleen and Various Legends and Lyrics, 1892 (first published 1890)
sets.headnote: W. B. Yeats was an Irish poet. He wrote this lyric in 1888 while living in London, after a shop-window fountain reminded him of the lakes of County Sligo, where he spent much of his childhood. Innisfree is a small island in Lough Gill.
sets.body:
I will arise and go now, and go to Innisfree,
And a small cabin build there, of clay and wattles made:
Nine bean-rows will I have there, a hive for the honey-bee,
And live alone in the bee-loud glade.

And I shall have some peace there, for peace comes dropping slow,
Dropping from the veils of the morning to where the cricket sings;
There midnight's all a glimmer, and noon a purple glow,
And evening full of the linnet's wings.

I will arise and go now, for always night and day
I hear lake water lapping with low sounds by the shore;
While I stand on the roadway, or on the pavements grey,
I hear it in the deep heart's core.

questions.model:
Yeats makes the peace of Innisfree something you can hear. The slow rhythms, repetitions and soft sounds act out the calm the speaker longs for, so we experience the island's tranquillity even though he is still stuck in the city.

The rhythm is unhurried from the first line. Long lines with a pause near the middle, like "I will arise and go now, and go to Innisfree", move like a measured chant, and the archaic, biblical "I will arise and go" gives the decision a solemn weight. Each stanza then ends with a shorter line, "And live alone in the bee-loud glade", which settles it like a breath out. "bee-loud" is a striking piece of sound imagery: the island isn't silent, it's full of a steady natural hum.

In the second stanza peace becomes almost physical. "For peace comes dropping slow, / Dropping from the veils of the morning to where the cricket sings". Repeating "dropping" across the line break slows us down, so peace seems to fall gradually, like dew or mist. "the veils of the morning" adds softness, and the stanza moves through the day, from "midnight's all a glimmer" to "noon a purple glow" to "evening full of the linnet's wings". The gentle list imitates time passing slowly in a place with no urgency.

The final stanza turns the music up. "I hear lake water lapping with low sounds by the shore" is full of l sounds and long vowels that copy the soft, regular movement of water against the bank. He hears it "always night and day", and in the last line the sound moves inward: "I hear it in the deep heart's core", where four heavy stresses slow the voice almost to a stop. Ending on sound rather than sight suggests peace is something felt inside, and the poem's music lets us share that inner experience.

sets.title: “Hope” is the thing with feathers
sets.author: Emily Dickinson
sets.source: “Hope” is the thing with feathers (c. 1861), first published in Poems, Second Series, 1891; text from the poet's manuscript version
sets.headnote: Emily Dickinson was an American poet who lived most of her life in her family home in Amherst, Massachusetts, and published almost nothing in her lifetime. The dashes and capital letters in this short lyric are her own.
sets.body:
“Hope” is the thing with feathers –
That perches in the soul –
And sings the tune without the words –
And never stops – at all –

And sweetest – in the Gale – is heard –
And sore must be the storm –
That could abash the little Bird
That kept so many warm –

I've heard it in the chillest land –
And on the strangest Sea –
Yet – never – in Extremity,
It asked a crumb – of Me.

It "sings the tune without the words": hope comforts by instinct, beyond reason or explanation. It "never stops – at all", which suggests constancy, and it has even "kept so many warm". The metaphor ends on hope's generosity. Although the speaker has carried it through hard times, "It asked a crumb – of Me." Unlike a real bird, which has to be fed, hope keeps us going and asks for nothing back.

questions.model:
Dickinson's punctuation and form slow us down and make us feel the weight of single words, so a simple, hymn-like poem becomes reflective and emphatic.

The dashes are her signature. In "And never stops – at all –", the pause isolates "at all" and turns a throwaway phrase into a firm declaration that hope never lets up. In "Yet – never – in Extremity," "never" is fenced in on both sides, as if she stops to insist on it. The dashes also copy the stop-start movement of thought, as though she is weighing each word, and they leave many lines open-ended, as if the song carries on past them.

The form is just as deliberate. The short quatrains and alternating line lengths echo the common metre of church hymns, which gives the poem a familiar, consoling music that suits a subject like hope. But slant rhymes such as "storm" and "warm" or "Sea" and "Me" unsettle the pattern, so the poem sounds harmonious but not quite resolved, like hope in a hard world.

Capitals add emphasis. "Gale", "Sea" and "Extremity" become forces, and the capitalised "Me" at the very end puts the speaker herself in the final position. The voice sounds simple, but it makes us linger on every turn of thought.

questions.model:
The view is mostly convincing, but it needs refining. Dickinson presents hope as remarkably durable, outlasting any hardship the speaker has known, yet she also admits hope is small and that a bad enough storm could shake it. Its strength is persistence, not power.

The poem's central claim is that hope never gives up. It "never stops – at all", and the dash and the final position of "at all" make that sound absolute. Hope is heard most clearly in hard times: "And sweetest – in the Gale – is heard". That paradox matters. The song is sweetest when conditions are worst, so hardship doesn't weaken hope; it shows what hope is worth.

But Dickinson doesn't make hope invincible. The bird is "little", made of feathers, and "And sore must be the storm – / That could abash the little Bird" admits that some storm could, in principle, unsettle it. "abash" means to disconcert or shame, not destroy, so even at worst hope is only silenced for a moment. Hope isn't stronger than hardship in raw force. It would take an extraordinary hardship to overcome it, and it has "kept so many warm" through ordinary ones.

The final stanza grounds the claim in personal experience. "I've heard it in the chillest land – / And on the strangest Sea –": the superlatives suggest the most extreme isolation and uncertainty, and the speaker has found hope in both. Then the closing lines add a different kind of strength: "Yet – never – in Extremity, / It asked a crumb – of Me." Hope isn't only resilient but completely unselfish, asking for nothing even when she has nothing to give.

So Dickinson suggests hope is a comfort that outlasts hardship rather than one that defeats it. Admitting its smallness and vulnerability makes its persistence more moving, and the poem's picture of hope ends up both realistic and deeply consoling.

sets.title: When You Are Old
sets.author: W. B. Yeats
sets.source: When You Are Old, in The Countess Kathleen and Various Legends and Lyrics, 1892
sets.headnote: W. B. Yeats wrote this lyric in 1891, loosely adapting a sonnet by the French Renaissance poet Pierre de Ronsard. It is usually read as addressed to Maud Gonne, the Irish revolutionary whom Yeats loved for many years and who repeatedly refused his proposals of marriage.
sets.body:
When you are old and grey and full of sleep,
And nodding by the fire, take down this book,
And slowly read, and dream of the soft look
Your eyes had once, and of their shadows deep;

How many loved your moments of glad grace,
And loved your beauty with love false or true,
But one man loved the pilgrim soul in you,
And loved the sorrows of your changing face;

And bending down beside the glowing bars,
Murmur, a little sadly, how Love fled
And paced upon the mountains overhead
And hid his face amid a crowd of stars.

Others loved her "moments of glad grace" and "your beauty with love false or true", a love tied to youth and looks, and maybe not even sincere. "But" sets the speaker apart: he "loved the pilgrim soul in you", her restless, searching spirit, and "the sorrows of your changing face". "loved" comes four times, so the stanza reads like a list of devotions that ends with his, the only one that takes in her sadness and her ageing. His love is deeper and more lasting because it doesn't depend on a beauty time will take away.

questions.model:
Yeats imagines the woman in old age, and that turns the speaker's present, unreturned love into a quiet prophecy of what she will one day understand. The tone that results is tender regret.

The opening picture is gentle and domestic: "When you are old and grey and full of sleep, / And nodding by the fire". The string of "and"s slows the line down to the drowsy pace of age, and the fireside suggests comfort, not decay. There is no bitterness. He imagines her old age with care.

"take down this book" points back at the poem itself. He imagines his words outlasting their love affair and taking her back to memories of "the soft look / Your eyes had once". The poem becomes a container for memory, and its quiet confidence suggests he knows she'll recognise its value too late.

The final stanza deepens the regret. Bending "beside the glowing bars" of the fire, she will "Murmur, a little sadly", an understatement that implies sorrow without despair. Then Love itself is personified: he "fled / And paced upon the mountains overhead / And hid his face amid a crowd of stars". The imagery rises from the hearth to the sky, so lost love becomes vast, remote, almost divine. It hasn't been destroyed, only withdrawn out of reach. Putting the intimate fireside next to the distant stars captures the tone exactly: a tender, wistful recognition of something precious that was offered and not taken.

questions.model:
The speaker is devoted, but not completely selfless. His love is real, yet the poem is also a gentle piece of persuasion that asks to be remembered.

There is strong evidence for selflessness. He loves "the pilgrim soul in you" and "the sorrows of your changing face", things that don't flatter him and will outlast her youth. He pictures her old age tenderly, "nodding by the fire", with no wish to see her suffer.

The poem's structure, though, hints at self-interest. It's a series of instructions, "take down this book, / And slowly read, and dream", imagining her reading his words and realising what he was worth. Setting himself against the many who loved her "with love false or true" implies he alone was sincere, and the final picture of her murmuring "a little sadly" imagines her regretting that she turned him down.

The most convincing reading is that both attitudes exist together. His love is real, but he wants it understood, even if only too late, and the tenderness of the tone softens what is really a plea.

sets.title: Dover Beach
sets.author: Matthew Arnold
sets.source: Dover Beach, in New Poems, Macmillan, 1867 (probably written c. 1851)
sets.headnote: Matthew Arnold was an English poet and critic. The poem is set at night at Dover, on the English Channel, and is spoken to a companion, probably his wife. It was written as scientific discoveries were unsettling traditional religious belief in Victorian England.
sets.body:
The sea is calm to-night.
The tide is full, the moon lies fair
Upon the straits;—on the French coast the light
Gleams and is gone; the cliffs of England stand,
Glimmering and vast, out in the tranquil bay.
Come to the window, sweet is the night-air!
Only, from the long line of spray
Where the sea meets the moon-blanch'd land,
Listen! you hear the grating roar
Of pebbles which the waves draw back, and fling,
At their return, up the high strand,
Begin, and cease, and then again begin,
With tremulous cadence slow, and bring
The eternal note of sadness in.

Sophocles long ago
Heard it on the Ægæan, and it brought
Into his mind the turbid ebb and flow
Of human misery; we
Find also in the sound a thought,
Hearing it by this distant northern sea.

The Sea of Faith
Was once, too, at the full, and round earth's shore
Lay like the folds of a bright girdle furl'd.
But now I only hear
Its melancholy, long, withdrawing roar,
Retreating, to the breath
Of the night-wind, down the vast edges drear
And naked shingles of the world.

Ah, love, let us be true
To one another! for the world, which seems
To lie before us like a land of dreams,
So various, so beautiful, so new,
Hath really neither joy, nor love, nor light,
Nor certitude, nor peace, nor help for pain;
And we are here as on a darkling plain
Swept with confused alarms of struggle and flight,
Where ignorant armies clash by night.

He even invites his companion to share it: "sweet is the night-air!" Then "Only" shifts us from sight to sound. He asks her to "Listen!" to "the grating roar / Of pebbles", and the harsh "grating" disturbs the peace. "Begin, and cease, and then again begin" copies the endless motion of the waves, which bring "The eternal note of sadness in". Under the calm surface, he hears a sadness that never goes away.

questions.model:
Arnold turns the real sea at Dover into an extended metaphor for religious faith. The ebbing tide becomes belief draining away from the modern world, leaving it exposed and comfortless.

The first stanza prepares the ground, as the speaker hears in the waves "The eternal note of sadness". The second widens it to human history: Sophocles heard the same sound and thought of "the turbid ebb and flow / Of human misery". The tide's movement becomes a pattern of human suffering, so the sea is already a symbol before Arnold names it.

In the third stanza he names it: "The Sea of Faith / Was once, too, at the full". Back then faith wrapped the world "like the folds of a bright girdle furl'd", a simile of protection, unity and brightness, as if belief held the world together like a belt. "Was once" tells us straight away that this time has passed.

The present is captured in sound: "But now I only hear / Its melancholy, long, withdrawing roar". The string of adjectives and long vowels stretches the line out, acting out the slow retreat of the tide and the speaker's drawn-out grief. "Retreating, to the breath / Of the night-wind" runs over the line break and carries the sound off into the dark. What's left is "the vast edges drear / And naked shingles of the world", a bare pebbled beach that suggests a world stripped of meaning and protection. The inverted "edges drear" and the word "naked" make the loss feel cold and vulnerable.

This was written when geology and evolutionary science were challenging literal readings of scripture, and the metaphor captures a whole culture in crisis. Arnold isn't arguing against faith; he's mourning its retreat. By rooting a spiritual loss in the sound and sight of an ebbing sea, he makes doubt something we can hear and feel.

questions.model:
Once religious faith has gone, the poem suggests, the only thing people can hold on to is being faithful to each other, and even that refuge is fragile.

The final stanza turns from the sea to his companion: "Ah, love, let us be true / To one another!" The exclamation makes loyalty an urgent necessity, not a romantic gesture. Faithfulness between two people takes the place of the lost "Sea of Faith".

They need it because the world deceives. It "seems / To lie before us like a land of dreams, / So various, so beautiful, so new", but "Hath really neither joy, nor love, nor light". The long list of negatives strips away every comfort, right down to certainty and "help for pain".

The closing image shows how small their refuge is. The lovers stand "as on a darkling plain" where "ignorant armies clash by night", a picture of confusion and pointless violence. So the poem offers human love as the one light left, but a light kept going in darkness and danger.

sets.title: I Will Fight No More Forever
sets.author: Chief Joseph (Nez Perce)
sets.source: Surrender speech, Bear Paw, Montana Territory, 5 October 1877, as recorded in English by Lt Charles Erskine Scott Wood; printed in Harper's Weekly, 17 November 1877
sets.headnote: Chief Joseph was a leader of the Nez Perce people of the American Northwest. In 1877, after a retreat of more than 1,500 miles from the US Army, the Nez Perce were surrounded near the Canadian border. This is the English version of his surrender message to General Oliver Howard, delivered through an interpreter; historians debate how closely the recorded words match what he said.
sets.body: Tell General Howard I know his heart. What he told me before, I have it in my heart. I am tired of fighting. Our chiefs are killed. Looking Glass is dead. Too-hul-hul-sote is dead. The old men are all dead. It is the young men who say yes or no. He who led on the young men is dead. It is cold, and we have no blankets. The little children are freezing to death. My people, some of them, have run away to the hills, and have no blankets, no food; no one knows where they are—perhaps freezing to death. I want to have time to look for my children and see how many of them I can find. Maybe I shall find them among the dead. Hear me, my chiefs. I am tired; my heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever.

questions.model:
The speech conveys defeat and dignity together with remarkable force, because Joseph admits total loss without ever giving up his authority or his self-respect.

He states defeat with complete honesty. "I am tired of fighting" begins the admission, and the personal part of the speech closes with "I am tired; my heart is sick and sad." The roll call of the dead and the children "freezing to death" make it clear the Nez Perce can't go on. He makes no attempt to disguise the loss.

Yet everything is framed with dignity. He opens not by pleading but with a message between equals: "Tell General Howard I know his heart." Joseph speaks as one leader to another, trusting Howard's earlier word. His concern isn't for himself but for his people: "I want to have time to look for my children and see how many of them I can find." "Hear me, my chiefs" shows he is still leading, explaining his decision to the people he is responsible for.

The last sentence brings the two together in a single line. "From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever" marks the moment of surrender with an image from the natural world, giving it the solemnity of an oath. "no more forever" accepts defeat completely, but it is presented as his own decision, made freely and calmly.

We should remember that these words reached their audience through an interpreter and a recorder, so some of their polish may come from translation. Even so, the plain, measured voice that survives makes defeat feel noble rather than humiliating, which is why the speech still moves people.

sets.title: Letter to Mrs Bixby
sets.author: Abraham Lincoln
sets.source: Letter to Mrs Lydia Bixby, 21 November 1864, printed in the Boston Evening Transcript, 25 November 1864
sets.headnote: During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln sent this letter of condolence to a Boston widow believed to have lost five sons fighting for the Union. Later research showed that two of the sons had died; some historians think Lincoln's secretary John Hay drafted the letter.
sets.body:
Dear Madam,—I have been shown in the files of the War Department a statement of the Adjutant General of Massachusetts that you are the mother of five sons who have died gloriously on the field of battle. I feel how weak and fruitless must be any word of mine which should attempt to beguile you from the grief of a loss so overwhelming. But I cannot refrain from tendering you the consolation that may be found in the thanks of the Republic they died to save. I pray that our Heavenly Father may assuage the anguish of your bereavement, and leave you only the cherished memory of the loved and lost, and the solemn pride that must be yours to have laid so costly a sacrifice upon the altar of freedom.

Yours, very sincerely and respectfully,
A. Lincoln.

questions.model:
The letter starts its comfort by admitting that comfort is almost impossible. Lincoln feels "how weak and fruitless must be any word of mine which should attempt to beguile you from the grief of a loss so overwhelming." "weak and fruitless" is humble, and "beguile" suggests words could only distract her, not heal her. Recognising the size of her loss first stops him from sounding glib.

The turn comes with "But I cannot refrain from tendering you the consolation". "Cannot refrain" suggests he feels personally obliged, and "tendering" is formal and respectful, as if he were offering a gift. And the comfort he offers isn't his own. It lies in "the thanks of the Republic they died to save" and in a prayer that "our Heavenly Father may assuage the anguish". By placing the consolation in the nation and in God rather than in his own eloquence, he stays true to the humility of his opening while still giving the mother something to hold on to.

questions.model:
I find the view persuasive. The letter genuinely honours the mother's grief, but it also frames that grief in a way that supports the Union's war effort, and the two purposes are so closely woven together that they're hard to pull apart.

Its respect for private grief is clear. It acknowledges "a loss so overwhelming" and admits that any words must be "weak and fruitless". It prays that God will "assuage the anguish of your bereavement", naming her pain directly instead of brushing it aside. The hope that she will keep "the cherished memory of the loved and lost" is tender, treating her sons as people she loved, not just as soldiers.

Yet the letter also gives these deaths a national meaning. The sons "died gloriously on the field of battle", and "gloriously" presents death in war as honourable. The comfort offered is "the thanks of the Republic they died to save", which recasts private loss as a contribution to a cause and quietly justifies what the war costs. The final metaphor makes this clearest: she is to feel "the solemn pride that must be yours to have laid so costly a sacrifice upon the altar of freedom." The altar makes her sons' deaths a sacred offering, and "must be yours" gently tells her what to feel. Her grief is to come with pride, even be transformed by it.

Context strengthens this reading. The letter was printed in a Boston newspaper within days, so it reached the public at a time when the Union needed continued support for the war, and its talk of glory and freedom would have spoken to every grieving family. It later emerged that not all five sons had died for the Union, an irony suggesting the letter's symbolic purpose mattered as much as its facts.

So the letter does both at once. Its humility and compassion are real, but its consolation can't be separated from a national story of sacrifice, and that is exactly what makes it such a powerful public document.

sets.title: Sonnet 18 (Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?)
sets.author: William Shakespeare
sets.source: Sonnet 18, in Shake-speares Sonnets, Thomas Thorpe, 1609 (spelling modernised as in standard editions)
sets.headnote: William Shakespeare's 154 sonnets were published in 1609. Sonnet 18 belongs to a group addressed to a young man whom the speaker admires; in Elizabethan English a 'lease' is a fixed-term rental and 'thou ow'st' means 'you own'.
sets.body:
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer's lease hath all too short a date;
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm'd;
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance or nature's changing course untrimm'd;
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow'st;
Nor shall Death brag thou wander'st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow'st:
So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

questions.model: The speaker raises a conventional comparison only to throw it out. His answer to his own question is that the beloved is "more lovely and more temperate": more beautiful and more even-tempered. Summer has flaws. It's unstable, since "Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May", and it's brief: "summer's lease hath all too short a date", a legal metaphor that makes summer something rented for a limited term. Even the sun is unreliable, "Sometime too hot" and often "dimm'd" by cloud. Listing summer's faults turns a familiar compliment into a bigger one: the beloved outdoes the best that nature has to offer.

questions.model:
For eight lines the sonnet dwells on decline: summer fades and "every fair from fair sometime declines". At line 9 the volta reverses that: "But thy eternal summer shall not fade". The beloved's beauty becomes a summer that never ends, an oxymoron that defies the natural cycle just described.

The third quatrain takes the defiance all the way to death. "Nor shall Death brag thou wander'st in his shade" personifies Death as a boaster who will be denied his win, and the run of negatives, "shall not", "Nor lose", "Nor shall", builds certainty. The reason comes in the next line: the beloved will live "When in eternal lines to time thou grow'st". "lines" puns on lines of poetry and on family lineage, but the couplet makes the main meaning clear.

The couplet is balanced and emphatic: "So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee." The parallel "So long" clauses stretch the claim across all of human time, and the repeated "this" points at the sonnet itself. The poem has shifted from praising the beloved to praising its own power. Poetry, not nature, is what grants immortality.

questions.model:
The sonnet suggests that time always destroys natural beauty, but that art can rescue beauty from time by fixing it in words that outlast the body.

For the first eight lines, time rules everything beautiful. Summer exists on a "lease" with "all too short a date", and the sun's "gold complexion" is "dimm'd". The general law is stated plainly: "every fair from fair sometime declines, / By chance or nature's changing course untrimm'd". Whether by accident or by nature's ordinary processes, beauty gets stripped away. It isn't something you own; it's on loan.

Art arrives as the answer to that law. The beloved's "eternal summer shall not fade" because they will live "in eternal lines", growing alongside time instead of being eaten by it. "grow'st" is a striking verb: in poetry the beloved doesn't decline but increases, reversing nature's pattern. The couplet makes the claim universal: "So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee." Art's life depends only on readers, and as long as there are readers it gives life.

So beauty is the subject, time the enemy and art the winner. There is an irony, though. The beloved is never named or physically described, so what survives isn't the person but the poem's praise. The sonnet's confidence is partly a claim for poetry itself. Shakespeare's verse really has outlived its subject, which suggests art's true victory over time is its own survival, carrying beauty forward as an idea rather than a living face.
